The Bluish-slate antshrike (Thamnomanes schistogynus) is a medium-sized antbird inhabiting humid lowland forests of the western Amazon basin. Available data on its metabolic physiology indicate a resting oxygen consumption of 61.82 milliliters per hour [JOi = 61.82 milliliters per hour] when measured at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value that reflects the species' typical thermal environment during active foraging periods. This basal oxygen consumption rate, recorded under standard respirometry protocols in captive individuals, is consistent with metabolic expectations for a passerine of this body size. Field studies tracking marked individuals reveal that females reach an ultimate body mass of 17 grams [Wwi = 17 grams], while males attain a slightly larger adult size of 18 grams [Wwi = 18 grams], a modest sexual dimorphism typical of many thamnophilids. Newly hatched nestlings emerge at an initial wet weight of just 2.41 grams [Ww0 = 2.41 grams], a value that underscores the altricial condition of this species and the substantial parental investment required to bridge the gap between this tiny neonatal mass and the adult target size. Comparative data from the congeneric Dusky-throated antshrike Thamnomanes ardesiacus provide a reference point for early-life development in this genus.

Incubation and early developmental stages of the Bluish-slate antshrike have been studied primarily through observations at active nests in undisturbed forest tracts. Based on closely related species such as Thamnomanes ardesiacus, the incubation period is estimated at 11.5 days [ab = estimated at 11.5 days] when eggs are maintained at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], the typical temperature of an attended nest in the shaded understory. This relatively short incubation reflects the intense nest predation pressure characteristic of Neotropical lowland forests, where accelerated embryonic development reduces the window of vulnerability. Following hatching, the nestling period culminates in fledging, which, again drawing on data from Thamnomanes ardesiacus, occurs approximately 11 days after hatching [tx = approximately 11 days after hatching] under the thermal conditions prevailing in at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]occupied nests. The transition from a downy, dependent chick to a flight-capable juvenile is thus remarkably rapid, consistent with a broader life-history strategy that prioritizes early departure from the nest. The period of post-fledging parental care and subsequent juvenile dispersal in this species remains poorly documented, though it is presumed to extend for several weeks as young birds develop foraging proficiency.

The chronology of reproductive maturation in the Bluish-slate antshrike has been inferred from long-term capture-recapture data and from behavioral observations of color-banded populations in southeastern Peru. Under the thermal regime characteristic of its active metabolic period, which averages approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], sexual maturity is attained at 37.5 days after hatching [tp = 37.5 days after hatching]. This remarkably short interval to puberty is notable among understory insectivorous passerines and likely reflects the high adult mortality rates and strong selective pressure for early reproduction in this lineage. The first successful breeding event, however, is delayed considerably relative to the onset of gonadal maturity. This discrepancy between physiological readiness and actual reproductive onset offers a compelling subject for further investigation.

Lifespan estimates for the Bluish-slate antshrike derive from mark-recapture studies conducted over a decade at a single site in Madre de Dios, Peru. The oldest documented individual in this population reached an age of approximately 8.2 years [am = approximately 8.2 years], though this value was recorded under the ambient temperature conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that prevail during the active season. This maximum longevity places the species in an intermediate position among Neotropical understory passerines, whose lifespans typically range from four to twelve years depending on body size and predation risk. Annual survival rates estimated from the same dataset suggest that adult mortality is relatively constant across age classes, with no evidence of pronounced senescence until the final year of life. The species' comparatively modest lifespan, set against its early age at sexual maturity and rapid reproductive schedule, points toward a life-history strategy that emphasizes early and sustained breeding over extended somatic persistence. Future demographic modeling would benefit from additional capture data across a broader geographic range.

Reproductive output in the Bluish-slate antshrike follows a pattern typical of many thamnophilid antbirds. At an ambient temperature of approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] during the active season, females produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = a single clutch per year], comprising two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], a modest annual fecundity that is compensated by relatively high nest success rates in undisturbed habitats. This annual reproductive rate, coupled with the species' early maturation and substantial adult lifespan, yields a lifetime reproductive output that appears sufficient to maintain stable populations in continuous forest. Nest placement in low forks of understory shrubs may reduce predation risk, though brood parasitism by cowbirds has been documented in fragmented landscapes. The trade-off between egg size and clutch size, constrained by the female's adult body mass of 18 grams [Wwi = 18 grams], results in eggs that represent a substantial maternal investment relative to body size. Future work should examine whether females adjust clutch size in response to local food availability or to the age and experience of the breeding female. The interaction between reproductive timing and the pronounced dry-season peak in insect biomass warrants further attention as a potential driver of annual breeding schedules.
